newsitem.title: USA: DNC head Romer will not run for '98 Senate.
newsitem.headline: DNC head Romer will not run for '98 Senate.

text.p: Colorado's Democratic governor Roy Romer ended months of speculation Wednesday when he formally announced he will not run for the U.S. Senate next year, despite a push from President Clinton.

When the three-term governor was appointed chairman of the Democratic National Committee in January, he said he would probably not run in 1998 for the Senate seat now held by Republican Ben Nighthorse Campbell.

Romer is popular in Colorado and probably had the best chance of helping the Democrats win back the seat. "I know that game. I think I could win that race. I've done some polling," he told reporters in his office.
But he said he wanted to finish his term as governor without the distraction of running for elective office. "If you become a candidate everything you do becomes politicized."
He added that he has to work with a Republican legislature and wants to "make the most" of the 18 months he has left.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton and Romer had talked about Romer running for the Senate many times. "The president feels like he will be a strong candidate but respects his individual decision," McCurry said.

Romer's term as governor ends next year and Colorado's term limits law bars him from running for a fourth term. He said he discussed his decision with Clinton when Denver hosted the G7 Summit last weekend.

"He had an interest in my running -- as a president you want to get a majority in the Senate," he said, referring to the fact that there are only 45 Democrats in the Senate. But he also said Clinton told him to do what he felt was best.

Until Romer took over as head of the scandal-ridden Democratic party, speculation had been rife he would run for the Senate seat against Campbell, the Senate's only American Indian, who was elected as a Democrat in 1992 but switched to the Republican party.

The 68-year-old Romer did not rule out a Clinton administration appointment in the future. The former farmer and rancher also said he might like to go into business, particularly something in the non-profit arena.

While Romer has been successful in the Rocky Mountain region, he said the Democratic Party will have to shed its "tax and spend" image to broaden its following there. But he said he was confident a Democrat could win the Colorado Senate election next year.
While not endorsing anyone, he said U.S. Representative David Skaggs from the liberal stronghold of Boulder could win.
The other U.S. senator from Colorado is Wayne Allard, a Republican elected for first time in 1996.
